data.title: Off-duty senior ambulanceman dies after abseiling fall on Kowloon Peak
data.description:
An off-duty senior ambulanceman has died after falling from a cliff while abseiling in Hong Kong.
The Fire Services Department said on Friday that it had received a report at 2.33pm that a man had fallen from Kowloon Peak in Wong Tai Sin while abseiling.
Rescuers and a government helicopter searched the area and found an unconscious man at a nearby cliff. Another man with minor injuries was found on a nearby trail.
The department mobilised its mountain and high-angle rescue teams during the search and a drone was also deployed.
Both men were airlifted to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan for treatment. The unconscious man was later pronounced dead.
The department confirmed the two men were both off-duty senior ambulancemen.
“The department expressed its utmost sadness over the death of its member and extended condolences to his family members,” a spokesman said, adding that it would provide all possible help.

data.title: 2 Hongkongers held in Philippines for months after prison terms end
data.description:
The Chinese embassy in Manila has expressed concern over the cases of two Hongkongers who have remained in custody in the Philippines for months despite being discharged from prison, according to the Immigration Department.
The department confirmed on Friday night that it was handling the two cases following an appeal from a former lawmaker and a Hong Kong man who returned to the city on Tuesday after serving 26 years in a Philippine prison for drug offences.
The returned Hongkonger, Tang Lung-wai, met the two residents, surnamed Cheung and Ng, in prison. He said he had also been held for weeks at the same immigration facility in the country as the pair while he waited to be deported.
Tang said Cheung and Ng were both arrested over drug-related offences in 2000 and 2001 and had completed their jail terms.
The Philippines Bureau of Immigration issued deportation orders, seen by the South China Morning Post, to Cheung and Ng in March and June, respectively. Tang said the pair were still waiting to complete their identity confirmation process.
Tang said Cheung had his fingerprints taken for the first time after waiting for six months. Ng had his fingerprints taken six or seven times, but they had not been accepted.
Ng and Cheung both received 40-year jail sentences. Ng was supposed to have been discharged in January 2025 and Cheung in January this year. However, their transfers to immigration facilities were also delayed.

Former lawmaker Paul Tse Wai-chun, who had been helping Tang for years, also appealed on Facebook for an early return of both of them.
“I hope that the [Hong Kong] government and other lawmakers will continue to pay attention and help them return as soon as possible,” he said.
The Immigration Department was actively following up on two cases involving residents who had completed their sentences in the Philippines and required repatriation to Hong Kong, a spokesman said.
He said the department would provide feasible help and had been liaising on the cases with the Office of the Commissioner of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Chinese embassy in the Philippines, including verifying the identities of the individuals and issuing entry permit documents for their return.
“The [Chinese] embassy in the Philippines has also expressed concern over the relevant cases and will continue to liaise with the Philippine authorities to coordinate the relevant repatriation arrangements,” he said.
The department said the Hong Kong government had always attached great importance to cases involving residents detained or imprisoned outside the city, paying close attention to their legitimate rights and interests and striving to provide them with help.
Tang was convicted of drug possession in 2011 and handed a life sentence, which in the Philippines amounts to a maximum of 40 years in prison.
A Manila court ruled in July that Tang’s sentence would be commuted in view of his good conduct and he was ordered to be released and deported immediately.
Tang waited three weeks in the immigration facilities before he was deported on Tuesday after his family appealed to the Hong Kong government for help.

data.title: Hong Kong could overtake London as top arbitration hub in decade: Bar Association head
data.description:
Hong Kong could dethrone London as the top choice for arbitration within the next decade given the Asian city’s status as a global fundraising capital for businesses in mainland China and beyond, the head of the Bar Association has said.
Jose-Antonio Maurellet, chairman of the Hong Kong Bar Association, told the South China Morning Post on Friday that the city had enjoyed rapid growth in arbitration work, with high-stakes cases attracting elite international legal talent.
Hong Kong tied with Singapore as the second-most preferred arbitration seat globally last year in a survey by Queen Mary University of London, trailing only the British capital.
The total amount in dispute in arbitration cases administered by the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre, the city’s oldest arbitration body, last year was HK$117.7 billion (US$15 billion).

Maurellet said Hong Kong could overtake London’s arbitration crown in less than 10 years as the city was increasingly chosen to resolve high-value disputes linked to its role as an international capital-raising hub.
“What we see in Hong Kong actually is more and more big players from the United States or even London acting for clients in Hong Kong,” Maurellet said.
“It means we get to cross swords with the best from elsewhere.”
The association chief made the remarks after attending a ceremony in London to mark the opening of the legal year in England and Wales.
More than 100 senior figures from legal organisations from over 40 jurisdictions worldwide attended the event at Westminster Abbey on Thursday.
Maurellet explained that a key factor driving overseas interest in Hong Kong’s arbitration services was the international composition of the city’s arbitrators.

The senior counsel said one-third of arbitrators at the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre hailed from other common law jurisdictions such as England, Australia and New Zealand.
However, Maurellet acknowledged that some foreign practitioners still viewed Hong Kong primarily as a forum for China-related disputes.
“They’re quite interested in basically asking, well, is it all about China?” he said.
Maurellet stressed that the broader international scope of the city’s arbitration caseload should be highlighted to build global confidence.
“Although a big part of the business is China-related, and we all know the advantages of being bilingual, there’s also, as the pie grows bigger, a part of that pie is available for international lawyers,” he said.
He added: “We also have interesting new markets like Brazil, Indonesia and the United Arab Emirates, and I think that really raises quite a lot of interest.”
Maurellet said he had received more inquiries than anticipated regarding the Hong Kong-headquartered International Organisation for Mediation, with lawyers showing keen interest in its mandate to resolve interstate conflicts and asking how to join as mediators.
“I think for certain jurisdictions, which for whatever cultural or geographical reasons in the past would not have gone to the more traditional historical places where this sort of work was done, I think Hong Kong opens up one more option, so I think it’s seen extremely positively,” he said.

data.title: Cutting New World ties over 11 Skies averts ‘lose-lose’ deal: Airport Authority
data.description:
The Airport Authority has averted a “lose-lose situation” by terminating a nearly 50-year contract with Hong Kong developer New World Development for the 11 Skies commercial project, with most facilities set to open in 2028, the statutory body’s directors have said.
Julian Lee Pui-hang, the authority’s executive director for finance, said on Friday that the organisation could no longer work with a debt-ridden partner on the ambitious development and that the project needed to be brought forward.
He said the authority could adopt a “technical solution” of taking New World to court for failing to deliver the project, but it would come with pitfalls.
“We could have sought a settlement in court, but it sacrifices time, and we need to bring forward the development,” he said. “If we went for a technical solution, it risks a lose-lose situation.”
New World, which is owned by the Cheng family through private holding company Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, announced on Wednesday that it would return the project to the authority by surrendering the infrastructure.
As part of the move, the developer will pay a HK$2.3 billion (US$293 million) break-up fee, spending HK$1.05 billion to complete the remaining works and provide agreed services, and offering a HK$1 option to buy the company’s shares.
“The whole package represents the biggest efforts of the major shareholder [of New World],” Lee said. “We have tried to maximise what we get. The option is a bonus.”
The option for the authority to buy 750 million New World shares also came with a string of conditions that have raised questions about its feasibility.




Under the conditions, the authority can only exercise the option within three years and must buy the shares in one go.
When it buys the shares, it cannot breach any bank covenants and cannot exceed the controlling shareholder’s interest. The authority would also be required to hold onto its stake in the company until September 2032.
The 750 million shares already represent 29.8 per cent of New World’s total issued share capital of 2.52 billion shares.
Chow Tai Fook Enterprises holds roughly a 45 per cent stake in New World and has indicated it intends to maintain its control of the developer.
The exercise price of the option will be HK$2.25 billion, or HK$3 per share – nearly a 50 per cent discount to Friday’s closing price of HK$5.82.
“New World will have a series of movements to follow,” Lee said without elaboration.
The developer has been offloading assets and refinancing capital to cut debt after a liquidity crisis emerged in 2023. As of June 30 this year, its total debts stood at HK$143.3 billion and its net debt was HK$126.3 billion.
The terminated contract was signed by New World in 2018 and was originally supposed to end in 2066.
The termination has attracted controversy as the move means the authority will give up its entitlement to receive 20 per cent of guaranteed rent or revenue rent, depending on whichever was higher, of the gross revenue from 11 Skies from 2027 to 2066.
The handover is due to be completed by April next year.
The 11 Skies project was intended to complement the authority’s goal of developing Skytopia, a HK$100 billion landmark surrounding Hong Kong International Airport, featuring commerce, culture, leisure and entertainment elements.

Cissy Chan Ching-sze, the authority’s executive director for commercial, said 11 Skies would be renamed soon and given a new identity before management hunted for investors and tenants.
“It will no longer be a mall,” she said. “It will be an entertainment hub.”
Originally, the HK$20 billion 11 Skies development was expected to include three grade A office towers totalling 52,955 square metres (570,000 square feet), and about 247,000 square metres of retail and dining space, representing 70 per cent of the entire project.
In May, the South China Morning Post reported that signs had emerged of the authority having regained control of the project.
In the first half of this year, the company wrote off HK$18.32 billion in net impairment losses and provisions on 11 Skies, following HK$2.7 billion in the same period in 2025.
Chan said some spaces in one of the office towers had been leased, while the other two were pending tenant recruitment.
“We aim to attract companies that organise exhibitions to move from Wan Chai to leverage more exhibitions to be held at AsiaWorld-Expo,” she said, adding that other potential tenants include private wealth and insurance companies.
The retail and dining spaces were repurposed as a destination for entertainment, wellness and experiences.
She cited restaurants offering jet-fresh seafood, carting and pet-friendly areas and spaces dedicated to visitors’ experiences as examples.
Chan said key components of Skytopia would be completed in 2028.
These include most parts of 11 Skies, an autonomous transport system that connects the Hong Kong checkpoint of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge with Tung Chung MTR station, a 12,000 square metres waterfront piazza, a water recreation area and the expansion of nearby facilities at AsiaWorld-Expo.
AsiaWorld-Expo will add 100,000 square metres of exhibition space and a 20,000-seat super arena for concerts and other events.
Chan added that a section of the yacht bay berthing facilities was also expected to be ready for use in 2028.

data.title: China’s buying spree in ASML DUV gear prompts US calls for total export ban
data.description:
Chinese semiconductor plants amassed hundreds of immersion lithography machines worth billions of dollars in recent years, according to former US officials, who urged Washington and its allies to shut down further exports.
Chinese-owned fabs had acquired an estimated 343 immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems by early 2026, said a report published in late September by the Centre for Technology & Statecraft (CTS), a Washington research group established in August.
Co-authored by former US export control official Nicholas Brown and Saif Khan, a former White House and commerce department technology policy adviser, the study adds fresh data to the debate in Washington over whether Western allies should impose a total blockade on immersion DUV tools bound for China.
Blocked from buying Dutch toolmaker ASML’s most advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography tools, Chinese chipmakers have leaned heavily on immersion DUV systems – some models of which remain exempt from Western export bans – to produce sophisticated semiconductors.
The report estimated that about 270 of the machines acquired by Chinese-owned plants were ASML’s Twinscan NXT:1980i immersion DUV systems.
Though technically behind EUV, these tools can be adapted to manufacture 7-nanometre-class logic chips and advanced memory for artificial intelligence processors, including Huawei Technologies’ Ascend series, the authors said.
Chinese fabs spent over US$13 billion acquiring about 90 NXT:1980i machines in 2024 and another 89 in 2025, according to the report.
The purported buying spree is reflected in ASML’s financial disclosures. China accounted for 41 per cent of the Dutch firm’s net system sales by shipment destination in 2024 and 33 per cent in 2025.

Sales to China have since moderated, dropping to 19 per cent of ASML’s total in the first quarter of 2026 and 14 per cent in the second. ASML previously said that its high level of 2024 shipments was partly driven by fulfilling backlogged orders delayed by earlier supply chain constraints.
The Netherlands began requiring export licences for ASML’s NXT:2000i and more advanced immersion DUV systems in September 2023. Those models have since been effectively barred from China. It extended the licence requirement to the NXT:1980i a year later, but shipments of that model can still be approved case by case.
The report argued that this approach left a major loophole, warning that even tools sold for mature chipmaking nodes can be repurposed or relocated to advanced production lines.
To close the loophole, the authors recommended a complete China-wide ban on all immersion DUV equipment, alongside restrictions on replacement parts and servicing at advanced facilities. They suggested Washington coordinate with the Netherlands or unilaterally extend American export rules to foreign-made systems using US tech.
The push aligns with growing pressure in US Congress.
The bipartisan Match Act, introduced in April, seeks China-wide restrictions on sales and servicing for chipmaking equipment that China cannot easily manufacture at home – explicitly targeting immersion DUV tools. Senators renewed calls for its passage in September, and Khan publicly endorsed the bill earlier this year.
While cut-offs would have little immediate impact because Chinese fabs have already built up an inventory of imported tools, the authors argued that the long-term difference would be substantial.
Under the study’s most expansive theoretical projection, if China overcame other chipmaking bottlenecks and continued importing about 90 NXT:1980i systems a year, its DUV fleet could support an annual output of up to 434 million AI chips equivalent to Nvidia’s H100 by 2035. Halting new imports in 2027 would cap that ceiling at 153 million units, it said.

data.title: MTR Corp pays out HK$2.25 billion for high-speed rail construction delays
data.description:
The MTR Corporation will hand over HK$2.25 billion (US$287 million) to the Hong Kong government as a one-off settlement for the delayed completion of the high-speed rail line, while reaching a consensus to avoid a payout over hurdles affecting the Sha Tin to Central Link.
While the transport firm oversaw the design, construction, testing, and operation of the two projects, both are owned by the government and involved public funds.
Under the arrangements announced on Friday, the MTR Corp will pay the government, its majority shareholder, HK$2.25 billion for the delay to the commencement of the 26km (16.1-mile) local section of the cross-border High Speed Rail, which was completed in 2018.
But the MTR Corp and authorities also agreed not to pursue further claims over the Sha Tin to Central Link, as the rail firm had shouldered HK$2.8 billion in extra costs to address quality issues and delays.
The project, which connects Admiralty MTR station to stops at the Hong Kong-mainland Chinese border, was completed in 2022 after repeated delays and a scandal over the substandard construction of Hung Hom station.
“The government has been following up in a serious, rigorous and professional manner with [the MTR Corp] on its responsibilities as the project manager in respect of programme delays in the construction of the [high-speed rail and Shatin to Central Link] projects, in order to safeguard the legitimate interests of the government and the public,” the Transport and Logistics Bureau said.
A government spokesman said both parties had learned lessons from the delays and implemented a series of mechanisms to strengthen railway project governance, supervision and cost control.
Jeny Yeung Mei-chun, CEO of the MTR Corp, said the firm had encountered significant difficulties during the course of construction.
“The corporation has drawn lessons from the two projects and conducted reviews and rigorous follow-up in light of their specific circumstances,” she said.
“Drawing on our extensive experience in railway construction and operations, we will continue to provide the railway infrastructure critical to Hong Kong’s future development and support the city’s long-term sustainable growth.”

data.title: Legislators urge broader cooling-off law after abrupt Hotstone Yoga closure
data.description:
Hong Kong lawmakers have urged the government to widen the scope of a proposed statutory cooling-off law to cover more types of wellness market trends after the abrupt shutdown of the Hotstone Yoga chain, as claimed financial losses by customers rose to HK$3.9 million (US$497,030).
Their calls followed the government’s commitment to introduce a bill in the Legislative Council in the first half of next year that would establish a statutory cooling-off period for prepaid fitness and beauty contracts.
However, lawmakers said on Friday that the current proposals were too narrowly focused on fitness centres and beauty parlours, leaving consumers unprotected against evolving wellness trends.
Lawmaker Jeff Yiu Ming said the legislation needed to keep pace with shifting market trends, pointing out that fitness offerings now included kickboxing, Pilates and yoga.
“The government might need to define statutory terms with precision to ensure all emerging wellness concepts fall within the law’s purview,” he said.
Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah previously said authorities hoped to introduce the amendment bill to Legco in the first half of 2027, although timing remained subject to other agenda priorities.
The administration has proposed rolling out a statutory seven-day cooling-off period and a 14-day refund window for prepaid beauty and fitness contracts. It has also suggested exempting lower-value contracts to minimise disruption, with the threshold ranging from HK$3,000 (US$382) to HK$15,000 or above.
Lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu also urged the government to expand the scope of the legal framework to protect the rights of the public.
“We need a clear overarching legal framework covering all business-to-customer prepaid contracts for future services across all sectors,” he said.

Tang added that while government officials assured him that centres offering both yoga and general fitness classes would fall within the scope of the statutory cooling-off period, real-world market operations presented numerous grey areas.
Without explicit statutory coverage, “everyday consumers without a legal background are easily left in the dark,” he warned, acknowledging that broader restrictions would likely face pushback from the business sector.
A customer who identified herself only as Chan earlier told the South China Morning Post that she understood at least 500 customers had suffered financial losses due to the abrupt closure of Hotstone Yoga.
A closure notice, issued by law firm Cheung & Co and posted outside the studios, stated the chain was shutting down after careful consideration due to “business operations and other actual circumstances.”
It stated the company would cease operations at the end of regular business hours on Wednesday and included an email address for parties holding “rights, debts or other claims against Hotstone” to submit documents.
The notice added that affected staff could inquire with the relevant government departments about their rights and file related applications, and Hotstone would provide the necessary documents and information “where reasonably practicable” to facilitate procedures.
The company said it would pay outstanding wages for September and refund class fees from that month by October 5.
Most of Hotstone’s social media pages were disabled by Thursday afternoon.
According to its Threads account, the business operated for 10 years and had studios in Central, Causeway Bay, Aberdeen, Jordan, Tsuen Wan, Sha Tin and Kwun Tong.
It also claimed to be the first studio in Hong Kong to provide hot stone yoga sessions, stating it employed more than 100 veteran instructors to teach yoga, stretching, dance and gym classes.
The Consumer Council said that as of Friday 5pm, it had received 286 complaints related to the chain’s closure involving claimed losses of HK$3,909,444.
Police said they had received multiple reports since October 1 from individuals who claimed to have purchased class packages at a local yoga centre that abruptly closed.
The case will be referred to relevant departments for follow-up.

data.title: Developers vie to land plum HK$2 billion residential site in Ho Man Tin
data.description:
The sole residential site included in the Hong Kong government’s latest land sale programme has attracted interest from a host of major developers, with 10 tenders being submitted before a noon deadline on Friday.
Chinachem Group, Wheelock Properties, Kerry Properties and Sun Hung Kai Properties all confirmed to the South China Morning Post that they had submitted individual bids for the site on Fat Kwong Street in Ho Man Tin, Kowloon, while Sino Land issued a joint tender with Great Eagle Group.
Representatives from other developers including CK Asset Holdings, K Wah International, China Overseas Land & Investment and Poly Property were also seen submitting bids at a government office, according to media reports. The Land Department said it had received 10 tenders in total.
The site has a maximum gross floor area of 19,300 square metres (207,750 square feet) and is expected to accommodate about 250 flats. It was originally included in the government’s 2026-2027 land sale programme.
The successful bidder will be required to build an elderly care centre and a community centre at the site, as well as level the access road connecting the development to Fat Kwong Street.
Midland Surveyors director Alvin Lam said the site’s location in an established luxury residential neighbourhood, proximity to Ho Man Tin MTR station and moderate development scale could attract a range of developers, including smaller players.
The firm estimated the site’s value at about HK$2.39 billion (US$305 million), based on an expected land premium of HK$11,500 per square foot of gross floor area.
Lam said the site could accommodate a mid-to-high-end residential project, with upper-floor homes potentially enjoying open views and partial sea views. Its proximity to the Hong Kong Polytechnic University could also support rental demand, he added.
The heated competition for the Fat Kwong Street site comes as developers weigh limited opportunities to secure well-located urban land against still-cautious expectations for the property market.
Development Secretary Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said in July that the government would release just one residential site in the July-to-September quarter, arguing that other sources of housing supply would help keep the city on track to meet its targets.
The government has lowered its land premium revenue target for the 2026-2027 financial year to about HK$18 billion, while CBRE estimates actual revenue could reach HK$14 billion to HK$16 billion.
Developers have nevertheless continued to replenish their land banks as Hong Kong’s residential market shows signs of recovery after a prolonged downturn. Kerry Properties and Sino Land have been among the developers actively pursuing new development opportunities.
Earlier in September, a Sun Hung Kai Properties subsidiary won the tender for MTR Corporation’s Tuen Mun A16 Station Phase Two Property Development, with total investment costs projected to exceed HK$20 billion. The second phase’s residential portion spans 249,979 square metres and is expected to yield around 5,510 homes.
The broader bidder pool echoes a trend in recent land sales. In May, construction company Able Engineering secured rights to a Tung Chung residential site for HK$1.63 billion, beating five major developer groups with a bid that exceeded analysts’ estimates. Market watchers cited localised optimism and growing confidence among alternative investors for the higher-than-expected bid.

data.title: Hong Kong to raise helpers’ monthly minimum wage to HK$5,220
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities have raised the minimum wage for foreign domestic helpers by more than 2 per cent to HK$5,220 (US$665) per month, while their food allowance will be unchanged, citing “more favourable” socioeconomic factors.
The government announced on Friday that the current minimum wage of HK$5,100 for foreign domestic helpers, or FDHs, would be increased by 2.35 per cent, and the adjusted salary would apply to all such contracts signed on or after Saturday.
While most employers provided free food to their helpers, they could choose to pay a food allowance in lieu, with this amount to remain unchanged at no less than HK$1,236 per month, authorities added.
“In this year’s review, we comprehensively considered a basket of socio-economic factors in accordance with the established mechanism, including Hong Kong’s general economic performance and labour market conditions over the past year, near-term economic outlook, affordability of FDH employers and basic living needs of FDHs,” a spokesman said.
“Having carefully assessed and balanced the views of all parties, and comprehensively considered that this year’s socio-economic factors are more favourable than those at the time of last year’s review, the government has decided to suitably increase the [minimum allowable wage] to HK$5,220 per month.”
The government also said that the Immigration Department would still process employment contracts signed on or before Friday using the old threshold, provided that they were submitted by the end of the month.
The raise fell short of previously suggested levels, with the Hong Kong Federation of Asian Domestic Workers Unions earlier proposing raising the minimum monthly wage to HK$6,670 and the food allowance to HK$2,770. Employers, meanwhile, had called for a pay freeze.
Last year, the government raised the minimum wage by 2.2 per cent from HK$4,990, while keeping the food allowance unchanged.
The pay rise drew criticism from both sides.
Chrystie Lam Hau-yiu, president of employers’ group the Coalition of Global Home Service Sustainable Development, said the move could put more pressure on employers while also costing job opportunities for helpers.
“Many families are facing inflation, rents or mortgage payments, as well as costs for raising children and keeping domestic workers. I believed the government had not weighted in the real affordability of employers,” she said.
Lam, citing an earlier survey of 6,000 employers, warned that as many as 70 per cent might consider stopping hiring helpers following the pay rise. He called on the government to introduce tax allowances for expenses related to foreign domestic helpers and step up its crackdown on job-hopping.
Phobsuk Gasing, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Federation of Asian Domestic Workers Unions, said FDHs were generally upset about the “very tiny increase”, arguing that it amounted to no substantial raise after inflation was taken into account.
“We are especially frustrated by no increase in the food allowance. It has been HK$1,236 since the year of 2023,” she said, adding that those who received a food allowance in lieu had to spend about HK$1,000 a month on food.
“The Hong Kong government should inform the public what the indicators are in their decision on deciding the [minimum allowable wage] and food allowance.”

data.title: From stock losses to bond bets: 5 figures investors are watching in China
data.description:
A sell-off in technology stocks pushed mainland Chinese equities to their lowest level in more than a year, even as Beijing stepped up support for the economy with a key interest rate cut. At the same time, Chinese government bonds attracted fresh interest as US Treasury yields climbed to a new high.
Here are some figures that have captured market attention this week.
China’s CSI 300 Index hits 13-month low
Mainland China’s CSI 300 Index dropped 2.2 per cent on Monday to its lowest level since August 21 last year, while the technology-focused Star Market 50 index tumbled 4.1 per cent. A 31 per cent plunge in the Star Market 50 during the third quarter contributed to a 12 per cent decline in the CSI 300.
Mainland Chinese and Hong Kong stocks could face a bumpy road in the fourth quarter amid underwhelming stimulus measures, concerns over further interest rate increases and changing sentiment towards artificial intelligence-related investments, analysts said.
Key lending rate cut by 0.25 percentage points
China’s central bank cut the one-year pledged supplementary lending rate to 1.5 per cent from 1.75 per cent on Tuesday, aiming to encourage policy banks to provide funding for projects aligned with national priorities.
The move came alongside a mortgage interest subsidy programme for first-time homebuyers, offering an annualised interest subsidy of 1 percentage point for up to five years for loans with principals of up to 1 million yuan (US$149,000).
China’s 30-year bonds gain favour as US yields climb
Citi Research analysts on Monday recommended going long on China’s 30-year sovereign bonds, forecasting yields to fall towards 1.8 per cent, while the 10-year yield could decline to 1.6 per cent.
On Tuesday, yields on China’s 30-year special treasury bonds fell to an intra-day low of 2.11 per cent, while 10-year yields dropped to a one-year low of 1.68 per cent.
Meanwhile, the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury rose to 5.25 per cent on Tuesday, while the 30-year Treasury yield reached 5.56 per cent, its highest level since 2004.
Chinese vehicle exports projected to top 12 million units
The China Passenger Car Association, a government-backed industry group, forecast overseas sales of Chinese-made vehicles – including passenger cars, buses and lorries – to top 12 million units in 2026, up 44 per cent from last year’s 8.3 million.
The projected figure is 20 per cent higher than the previous estimate of 10 million vehicles made by the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
China’s R&D spending reaches 2.8 per cent of GDP
China’s spending on research and development exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (US$584.8 billion) in 2025, accounting for 2.8 per cent of gross domestic product.
For the first time, the country’s R&D expenditure surpassed the average among members of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, which stood at 2.7 per cent for the year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

data.title: Consumer spending picks up in Hong Kong, with retail sales rising 5.6% in August
data.description:
Hong Kong’s retail sales rose by 5.6 per cent year on year in August, with the latest figures showing consumer spending picking up after growth eased for two consecutive months.
Retail sales value reached HK$32 billion (US$4.1 billion), according to provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Friday. Sales in the first eight months of the year rose by 8.5 per cent compared with the same period in 2025.
“Growth was seen across many types of retail outlets, while online retail sales value grew notably, reflecting a continued shift in consumer spending towards digital channels,” a government spokesman said.
The latest figures followed a 4.5 per cent increase in July, when sales reached HK$31 billion, the lowest monthly value recorded in the first seven months of the year. Growth had slowed from 7.9 per cent in May to 4.6 per cent in June.
Sales of electrical goods and other consumer durables recorded the strongest increase in August, rising by 29.1 per cent year on year, followed by jewellery, watches and clocks, and valuable gifts, at 11.9 per cent.
Motor vehicles and parts recorded the steepest decline, falling by 22 per cent.
The Hong Kong Retail Management Association had previously warned that August sales fell short of expectations. Its survey, which covered about 3,100 shops and 75,000 employees, found that about 40 per cent of respondents reported weaker-than-expected performance.
Association chairwoman Annie Tse Yau On-yee said last month that foot traffic in traditional tourist districts remained healthy, but visitors’ spending power was still relatively weak.
Hong Kong’s economy grew by 4.3 per cent year on year in the second quarter, while private consumption expenditure rose by 2.8 per cent in real terms, down from 4.9 per cent in the preceding quarter.

data.title: Abby Choi struck with hammer during fake car trip to fetch daughter, court hears
data.description:
Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung died of head injuries after being hit with a hammer during a car journey she believed was to pick up her daughter from school, a court has heard.
Prosecutors on Friday detailed how three of Choi’s former relatives rented a remote village house and went on a shopping spree to acquire items they needed before allegedly killing the 28-year-old and disposing of her body on February 21, 2023.
Choi’s ex-husband Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial in the High Court after pleading not guilty to a joint count of murder.
Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body between February 21 and 23. His two sons pleaded guilty to the offence before the trial.
The murder allegedly arose from a family feud over the sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat at the upscale Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin.
The elder Kwong, the property’s registered owner, reportedly resented Choi for trying to sell the flat and enlisted his two sons to help kill the influencer so he could keep it for himself.
Prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC said the defendants showed significant pre-planning when they bought a wide variety of items between February 4 and 17 in preparation for the murder.
Those items included a 1lb (450 grams) ball-peen hammer – the alleged murder weapon – a commercial meat mincer, a 14-by-14-inch (36-by-36cm) soup pot, an electric saw, three knives, a second-hand refrigerator and multiple containers.
Draycott said Kwong Kau rented a 600 sq ft flat at Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village, where Choi’s body was dismembered, and asked a friend to rent a high-rise flat at The Arch in West Kowloon, which would be used as Alex Kwong’s hideout.
On the day of the alleged killing, Choi boarded a white Toyota Alphard driven by Anthony Kwong, who was working as her chauffeur at the time, under the impression that he would take her to a school in Pak Shek Kok where her then eight-year-old daughter was studying.
The prosecution alleged that during that trip, Alex Kwong, who was sitting on the left side of the back seat, used the hammer to hit Choi’s head, either killing her or rendering her unconscious.

Surveillance camera footage retrieved from Moko shopping centre in Mong Kok showed Anthony Kwong meeting Alex Kwong at a coffee shop shortly before the journey, during which the elder brother appeared to demonstrate to his younger sibling how to drag Choi by her hair and strike her in the head.
Draycott suggested that Choi could have been attacked shortly after 2.44pm on February 21, 2023, as her text conversation with her mother-in-law had come to an abrupt stop at that time.
The two brothers met up with their father outside the village house in Tai Po and discreetly carried a box believed to contain Choi’s body inside the flat after 3pm.
Draycott noted that Choi, who was 152cm (five feet) tall and weighed about 90lbs (41kg), was small enough for the accused to hide her body inside one of the plastic containers they bought in advance.
She also highlighted the trio’s unusually calm demeanour outside the village house, saying none of the accused appeared shocked or frightened by what must have been a violent attack inside the car.
“They were not worried. They were not upset. It was exactly what they expected to happen,” the prosecutor said.
Later that afternoon, Alex Kwong changed his clothes and left the village house on foot, “leaving his father Kwong Kau and his brother to clear up the mess”, according to the prosecution.
When the crime came to light on February 24, Choi’s head was found inside the soup pot and her legs inside the refrigerator. Flesh was also discovered inside a smaller pot and on a wooden chopping board, while multiple electric saws were seized from the premises.
Draycott said there was no evidence that any of the accused intended to cannibalise Choi’s body. “They cooked her to make her flesh unrecognisable,” she added.
The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

data.title: How Hong Kong stacks up against Singapore in race for next-generation wealth
data.description:
Hong Kong ranked seventh globally as a destination for attracting and retaining the next generation of high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs), trailing traditional rival Singapore in sixth place, according to a Savills study.
The two top finance hubs in the Asia-Pacific region have been stepping up efforts to strengthen their positions as regional wealth-management hubs amid an unprecedented global transfer of wealth between generations.
“Hong Kong offers many incentives similar to Singapore,” according to the global real estate adviser’s Next-Generation Wealth Hubs Index released on Thursday.
“It provides low taxation, financial sophistication, safety and connectivity, reinforcing its position as a leading hub for wealth preservation and family offices in Asia.”
The study focused on individuals under the age of 40 who have inherited significant fortunes, are expected to benefit from wealth transfers, or have built their own wealth through entrepreneurship.
New York topped the global rankings, followed by Miami and London, respectively, according to the report.
In the Asia-Pacific region, Tokyo ranked third, followed by Shanghai and Bangkok.
Residential real estate must now deliver more than capital preservation alone. It must support how wealth holders and their families want to live, work, travel, connect and plan for the future
Kelcie Sellers, Savills World Research
Residential real estate must now deliver more than capital preservation alone. It must support how wealth holders and their families want to live, work, travel, connect and plan for the future
Hong Kong was also home to 71 HNWIs under the age of 40 with net assets of at least US$5 million, making it the 12th-largest concentration in the world and the largest in Asia-Pacific, according to the study. It also defined HNWIs as those with partially valuated dossiers with total assets of at least US$2 million.
Singapore ranked 13th with 70 individuals in the same category.
“Recent trends suggest a shift in HNWI demographics, with a growing proportion of wealthy individuals from mainland China who are drawn to the high quality of life and ease of access,” the study said.
Hong Kong “acts as a key gateway to wider international markets, with one of the most active [initial public offering] markets in the world and has the highest proportion of millionaires relative to the population across [Asia-Pacific]”, Savills said.
Additionally, Hong Kong’s wealth-hub status was being strengthened by the city government’s continuing investment in “top-end medical facilities and yachting infrastructure”.
The report also cited Hong Kong’s lifestyle appeal, noting that it was home to 287 Michelin-listed restaurants and hosted prestigious sporting events annually.
The city is set to host the Hong Kong Open later this month at the Hong Kong Golf Club in Fanling, carrying a prize purse of US$2 million. The Bank of China Hong Kong Tennis Open, which has regularly attracted some of the world’s top men’s tennis players since its return in 2024, is scheduled for January.
Alongside the growth, a significant transfer of capital is under way. An estimated US$84 trillion was expected to transfer between generations over the next two decades, according to consulting company Capgemini, with US$72 trillion likely to pass directly to heirs, and a further US$12 trillion to philanthropic causes.
Younger wealth holders were becoming increasingly global in outlook and placed greater emphasis on factors including lifestyle, education, wellness and personal values when deciding where to live, invest and establish businesses, Savills said in a separate statement.
Kelcie Sellers, associate director at Savills World Research, said capital was likely to become increasingly selective as wealth moved across borders and generations.
“Scarce, turnkey and highly serviced assets in markets that combine legal stability, lifestyle quality, privacy and long-term liquidity are likely to remain most resilient,” Sellers said.
“Residential real estate must now deliver more than capital preservation alone. It must support how wealth holders and their families want to live, work, travel, connect and plan for the future.”
To identify locations best positioned to attract the next generation of global wealth, Savills assessed more than 100 wealth hubs across four key pillars – business, governance and connectivity; wealth clusters and local environment; wealth management and taxation; and lifestyle.

data.title: Hong Kong users caught off guard as Anthropic tightens VPN access to Claude
data.description:
US artificial intelligence company Anthropic appears to have stepped up enforcement of geographical restrictions on its Claude models in Hong Kong, with local users reporting abrupt account suspensions after accessing the service through virtual private networks (VPNs).
A wave of complaints surfaced on social media platforms X and Reddit on Thursday, as users who had operated accounts for months using VPNs found them suddenly disabled.
One Hong Kong-based user posted on the “r/claude” subreddit that they received an email from Anthropic’s safeguards team citing “suspicious signals” associated with their account, which would be revoked for usage policy violations.
“I used it with NordVPN from Hong Kong for six months and today this happened,” the user wrote, adding that they were trying to retrieve their conversation history and data.
While Anthropic has not publicly announced a new policy regarding VPNs, the sudden surge in suspensions suggests a deliberate tightening of long-standing regional restrictions. Hong Kong is excluded from Anthropic’s list of supported locations, alongside mainland China and Macau.

Despite these limits, tech-savvy users in the city had bypassed blocks by routing connections through supported markets like Singapore via VPNs and sometimes registering with foreign payment details.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday outside normal US business hours.
The apparent enforcement push comes amid growing friction between the San Francisco-based firm and Chinese developers. In a report published last month, Anthropic accused seven Chinese AI labs of conducting “industrial-scale” model distillation – harvesting outputs from Claude to train competing models.
Anthropic alleged that companies including Beijing-based Moonshot AI and Hangzhou-based DeepSeek circumvented geographic blocks using thousands of fraudulent accounts and third-party proxy networks.
Moonshot alone allegedly routed more than 23 million exchanges to Claude between May and July, disguised through accounts appearing to originate from Singapore and Japan. Beijing has rejected US allegations of AI distillation as groundless.
Geopolitical tensions have been growing around AI development.
In an essay last month calling on frontier labs to pace the release of advanced systems, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that a Chinese lead in AI would pose a “grave danger” to the world, urging Washington to maintain export controls on advanced semiconductors to China.

data.title: Mainland Chinese visitors pack Hong Kong malls on second day of National Day break
data.description:
Mainland Chinese visitors have flocked to Hong Kong’s shops and malls on the second day of the National Day “golden week” holiday, with some looking for outdoor gear and others browsing the city’s bookstores.
Hong Kong recorded over 277,300 mainland arrivals on Thursday – the first day of the week-long break – representing about 47 per cent of total inbound passengers for the day, according to immigration figures.
The city welcomed over 68,800 mainland arrivals on Friday as of 10am. By then, Mong Kok’s shopping districts were crowded with visitors and pedestrians. Beauty shops and tea restaurants were filled by noon, while a long queue formed at the entrance of Sim City, a shopping centre known for camera equipment.
David Liu Haibo, a university student from Hunan, came to Hong Kong with two friends for a hiking trip, which would include a visit to Grass Island.
Liu said on Friday morning that they were looking to buy outdoor gear at Grand Plaza in Mong Kok, as they had learned from the Chinese social media platform RedNote that the shopping centre was well-known for outdoor clothing and equipment.
“We’re each planning to spend around HK$2,000 (US$255) on windbreakers and outdoor backpacks,” Liu said.
“The Osprey outdoor backpacks especially, as they may cost about HK$500 to HK$600 more back on the mainland, and the Hong Kong dollar to yuan exchange rate is very favourable right now, saving us a lot of money.”

A 23-year-old Sichuan man surnamed Sheng was on a two-day trip in Hong Kong with friends. Instead of visiting shopping centres, he made bookstores his main stops, including Commercial Press and Joint Publishing.
His biggest purchase was a collector’s edition of the traditional Chinese novel Jin Ping Mei, which he said cost HK$1,580 and was not available on the mainland.
“I really enjoy historical folklore and popular fiction,” Sheng said, adding that the different volumes included commentaries by Huang Lin, a distinguished professor at Fudan University and president of the Chinese Jin Ping Mei Research Association.
“I really enjoy reading his commentaries, and I also have a version of Dream of the Red Chamber with his review.”
Wang, a visitor from Zhejiang, said she was part of a group comprising two families, including four children. They were visiting Hong Kong for two days and had spent about HK$2,000 on bags, medicine and cosmetics on the first day, she said.
Her two sons also wanted to buy sportswear, including football jerseys of teams such as Real Madrid.
Hong Kong is expected to welcome about 1.29 million mainland Chinese travellers over the golden week break, which lasts from October 1 to 7.
Additional reporting by Edith Lin

data.title: Rain dampens visitor numbers at Hong Kong attractions on day 2 of ‘golden week’
data.description:
Rain dampened visitor numbers at some of Hong Kong’s popular attractions on Friday morning, the second day of the National Day “golden week” holiday.
Queues at the Peak Tram terminus in Central remained short, with passengers waiting less than an hour to board.
Among them was Jasper Huang, a mechanical engineer in his twenties from Xiamen, Fujian province, who was visiting Hong Kong with friends for four days.
“We plan to visit some famous spots like Victoria Harbour and the streets of Central, and spend around HK$5000 (US$637) each person for sightseeing and food,” he said.
The group was staying at a hotel in Tsim Sha Tsui, with most of its itinerary focused on Hong Kong Island and Kowloon.
At the Peak Galleria, showers drove visitors indoors from the rooftop terrace. A 35-year-old visitor from Yunnan who gave only his surname, Liang, said the weather had taken some of the shine off the city views.

“It is a shame for the view, so I will go for indoor cultural spots instead, like Tai Kwun and the museums in West Kowloon,” he said.
Liang and his wife were staying at a hotel in Mong Kok. He said they would spend three days in Hong Kong, with a budget of up to HK$10,000 before returning to Yunnan to spend the rest of the holiday with family.
Another visitor, Li Ling-ling, an 18-year-old university student from Guangdong province, was staying with relatives during her four-day trip.
“I will visit the Avenue of Stars later, and on other days I will spend a few hundred on cosmetics and check out Kowloon attractions like Temple Street,” she said.
Hong Kong recorded more than 277,300 mainland Chinese arrivals on the first day of the holiday, which runs from Thursday to next Wednesday, according to Immigration Department figures. They accounted for about 47 per cent of total inbound passengers.
As of 10am on Friday, Hong Kong had recorded more than 68,800 arrivals from the mainland.

data.title: Return of 11 Skies project to Airport Authority will spur hub development: experts
data.description:
Hong Kong airport authorities’ move to take back the 11 Skies mall project will catalyse the development of its aviation hub, a government adviser and a hospitality sector expert have said, calling for better access and immersive entertainment to attract visitors.
Their remarks came on Friday, two days after developer New World Development (NWD) announced it would return the project to the Airport Authority next year – including an entertainment complex and three office towers – and provide cash or equivalents of over HK$3 billion (US$382.3 million), on the back of major losses.
Perry Yiu Pak-leung, a board member of the authority, supported the move, saying it had been pushing other projects under the Skytopia blueprint, which envisions building a destination with shopping, dining, hospitality, business and entertainment experiences.
He highlighted the AsiaWorld-Expo Phase 2 development, which includes an indoor arena with a seating capacity of over 20,000, as well as future yacht berths and other infrastructure and business activities under the blueprint.
“I believe that resolving the issue and reaching an agreement can enable us to achieve synergy and advance it faster,” Yiu told a radio show.
“The agreement can allow the project to kick off in 2028 … We are not required to raise extra funds for the initial capital. Under such circumstances, it has laid a solid foundation for the authority to advance the project.”
On Wednesday, the authority said it was taking forward the project “full steam ahead” and aimed to create a unique entertainment hub to be opened in 2028-29.
Yiu, who is also chairman of China Travel Service (Hong Kong), said 11 Skies would focus on offering innovative entertainment experiences currently lacking in the city, rather than on retail and catering services.
He cited the example of a collaboration between a go-karting facility and car brands, as well as leveraging the airport’s cold chain logistics to build a fresh food market with different products and cuisines.
“The public is looking for experience and immersive entertainment, rather than simple product sales and promotion,” he said.
Yiu also suggested improving the accessibility of the complex, noting that the airport should ensure smooth and quick transport for tourists.
He also highlighted the potential footfall brought by the Southbound Travel for Guangdong Vehicles scheme. Private cars under the scheme can park at the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge, allowing visitors to travel around the city or transfer flights.
“It can integrate with the fishing village culture and green tourism resources on Lantau Island, building it into an international tourism island,” he said.

Speaking on the same radio show, Dennis Wong Ka-wing, head of the Hong Kong Institute of Vocational Education’s department of hospitality, said the deal would boost tourism under the aviation hub blueprint.
But Wong pointed out that 11 Skies had little footfall, as surrounding sites were under construction and visitors had few incentives to go to the shopping centre.
“In the future, the authority can consider opening more walkways to divert footfall … It has a walkway connecting the AsiaWorld-Expo, but it does not have an obvious visitor route to the airport,” he said.
He also suggested that the authority provide parking at cheaper rates to entice locals to the mall.
“It can drive a huge amount of footfall and stimulate consumption. Whether they spend much or not, at least it can drive footfall and create a talking point among the community,” Wong said.
Apart from attracting tourists through the cross-border driving scheme, Wong said the authority should also focus on drawing crowds attending large-scale concerts and performances at the future AsiaWorld-Expo Phase 2 development.
He also saw the project’s potential for drawing high-end travellers, as its office buildings could provide premium medical services close to the airport.
Hotels and future berthing facilities in Skytopia could also attract high-spending tourists, Wong added.
NWD made the announcement as it entered its third year of deleveraging after liquidity concerns surfaced in 2023. The company has since stepped up asset disposals and capital recycling to improve liquidity and reduce leverage.

data.title: From stock losses to bond bets: 5 figures investors are watching in China
data.description:
A sell-off in technology stocks pushed mainland Chinese equities to their lowest level in more than a year, even as Beijing stepped up support for the economy with a key interest rate cut. At the same time, Chinese government bonds attracted fresh interest as US Treasury yields climbed to a new high.
Here are some figures that have captured market attention this week.
China’s CSI 300 Index hits 13-month low
Mainland China’s CSI 300 Index dropped 2.2 per cent on Monday to its lowest level since August 21 last year, while the technology-focused Star Market 50 index tumbled 4.1 per cent. A 31 per cent plunge in the Star Market 50 during the third quarter contributed to a 12 per cent decline in the CSI 300.
Mainland Chinese and Hong Kong stocks could face a bumpy road in the fourth quarter amid underwhelming stimulus measures, concerns over further interest rate increases and changing sentiment towards artificial intelligence-related investments, analysts said.
Key lending rate cut by 0.25 percentage points
China’s central bank cut the one-year pledged supplementary lending rate to 1.5 per cent from 1.75 per cent on Tuesday, aiming to encourage policy banks to provide funding for projects aligned with national priorities.
The move came alongside a mortgage interest subsidy programme for first-time homebuyers, offering an annualised interest subsidy of 1 percentage point for up to five years for loans with principals of up to 1 million yuan (US$149,000).
China’s 30-year bonds gain favour as US yields climb
Citi Research analysts on Monday recommended going long on China’s 30-year sovereign bonds, forecasting yields to fall towards 1.8 per cent, while the 10-year yield could decline to 1.6 per cent.
On Tuesday, yields on China’s 30-year special treasury bonds fell to an intra-day low of 2.11 per cent, while 10-year yields dropped to a one-year low of 1.68 per cent.
Meanwhile, the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury rose to 5.25 per cent on Tuesday, while the 30-year Treasury yield reached 5.56 per cent, its highest level since 2004.
Chinese vehicle exports projected to top 12 million units
The China Passenger Car Association, a government-backed industry group, forecast overseas sales of Chinese-made vehicles – including passenger cars, buses and lorries – to top 12 million units in 2026, up 44 per cent from last year’s 8.3 million.
The projected figure is 20 per cent higher than the previous estimate of 10 million vehicles made by the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
China’s R&D spending reaches 2.8 per cent of GDP
China’s spending on research and development exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (US$584.8 billion) in 2025, accounting for 2.8 per cent of gross domestic product.
For the first time, the country’s R&D expenditure surpassed the average among members of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, which stood at 2.7 per cent for the year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

data.title: New World Development posts HK$26.8b loss after 11 Skies terminationThe conglomerate booked HK$18.3 billion in impairments and provisions tied to the ill-fated mall project.
data.description:
New World Development (NWD) reported a net loss of HK$26.8 billion (US$3.42 billion) for the year ended June, as the developer booked HK$18.3 billion in impairments and provisions tied to the early termination of its flagship 11 Skies mall project.
Echo Huang, the firm’s chief executive, said at a Wednesday earnings briefing that the group had “met its targets over the past 18 months”, including focusing on its property business, improving cash flow and enhancing operating efficiency.
NWD will hand the 11 Skies project back to Airport Authority Hong Kong (AAHK) next year under an agreement reached on Wednesday, which will see the company face charges worth HK$18.3 billion.
The deal will see the developer pay a HK$2.3 billion early termination fee, hand over another HK$14.7 billion in non-cash impairments, and also make provisions for HK$1.05 billion worth of pre- and post-handover work.
The agreement ends NWD’s contractual involvement in the 11 Skies project – with its three office towers and entertainment complex handed over to AAHK at no cost – as Hong Kong’s most indebted major developer pushes ahead with its deleveraging efforts.
AAHK said it would now move “full steam ahead” with the 11 Skies project, aiming to create “a unique entertainment hub that contributes to the overall strategic development of Skytopia project”.
A Hong Kong government spokesman said the agreement enabled AAHK to move ahead with the project’s future development and that the Airport Authority would redefine the “positioning, theme, sector mix and operational model” of 11 Skies to align with the overall future development of Skytopia.
NWD management said in the statement that the termination would “reduce the group’s future financial commitments” related to the project and would not have a significant adverse impact on its financial position during the forecast period.
The group’s revenue dropped 28 per cent to HK$20 billion for the year, while core operating profit was HK$7.7 billion, up 28 per cent from a year earlier, reflecting stringent cost controls and improved margins, according to the company.

The results come as NWD enters its third year of deleveraging after liquidity concerns surfaced in 2023, when rising interest rates and reports of asset sales sent its perpetual and US-dollar bond prices sharply lower.
The company has since stepped up asset disposals and capital-recycling to improve liquidity and reduce leverage.
The company secured a HK$88.2 billion refinancing deal last year, extending more than HK$60 billion of debt due in 2025 and 2026 by three years and pushing its earliest maturity to June 2028.
Last week, it announced mainland property sales exceeding 1.7 billion yuan (US$240 million), including deals involving the Ningbo Tower and office and retail properties in Hangzhou. The group said the transactions would accelerate capital recycling and strengthen its financial resilience.
Total debt stood at HK$143.3 billion at the end of June, while net debt was HK$126.3 billion, bringing the net gearing ratio to 68.3 per cent, compared with 58.1 per cent a year earlier, according to the company.
Hong Kong home sales are another focus as NWD seeks to turn its residential pipeline into cash to reduce debt. Contracted sales in the city reached HK$22.1 billion during the year, up 101 per cent from a year earlier, as the city’s residential market rebounded.
The company did not declare a final dividend, keeping its full-year dividend suspended for a third year. NWD shares were up 1 per cent on Wednesday. The stock has fallen 19 per cent since the start of this year.
Additional reporting by Denise Tsang

data.title: DeepSeek effect? How China’s quant funds thrive amid tight regulatory scrutiny
data.description:
China’s quantitative investing sector has produced 18 funds managing more than 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) in assets each so far this year, underlining the industry’s ability to generate competitive returns despite a tight regulatory environment.
The firms are among 159 Chinese hedge funds overseeing more than 10 billion yuan in assets each, riding the technology-driven momentum in the world’s second-largest stock market.
Among the new entrants to the club were AXQ Capital, Hopeseek Fund and Huanian Fund, according to financial data provider Wind.
“Many quant funds are now doing exceptionally well,” said Christopher Beddor, deputy China research director at economic research firm Gavekal Dragonomics.
“Onshore equity markets are less sophisticated than major global markets,” Beddor said, so “quant funds can often generate solid returns by deploying systematic trading strategies that were first developed abroad”.
More Chinese investors are moving into financial assets due to low deposit rates and weak real estate performance
Gary Ng, Natixis
Gary Ng, economist at investment bank Natixis, said Chinese investors increasingly view hedge funds favourably.
“More Chinese investors are moving into financial assets due to low deposit rates and weak real estate performance,” he said.
Quant funds are also becoming more accessible. Chinese brokerages, such as Sinolink Securities and Shenwan Hongyuan Securities, have started promoting quant trading services through their mobile apps, allowing eligible investors to apply for access to China’s quant trading platforms.
Despite the quant funds’ competitive returns, China could be “a very tricky regulatory environment”, Beddor said.
Even though “China’s financial regulators are much more invested in market outcomes than regulators in other major markets,” they “can and do crack down on quant funds if they feel those firms may be contributing to market volatility”, said Beddor.
Beddor, however, pointed to DeepSeek, which was backed by Chinese quant fund High-Flyer, as possibly the turning point in how policymakers viewed quant funds.
“DeepSeek was created by a fund, not a traditional tech company,” he said. “Its breakthrough was the first time that policymakers seemed to have realised the fund industry could play a serious role in technological development.”
The top 18 quant funds took an average of 8.4 years to surpass the 10 billion yuan assets-under-management mark, although five reached the milestone in less than five years.
Chinese private securities investment funds, including but not limited to quant funds, managed more than 9 trillion yuan in assets as of the end of August, according to the Asset Management Association of China.
